en.title: Veterinary Medicine: the whole course
en.short: How veterinary medicine is organised, from basic sciences to clinical practice, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach veterinary concepts to students. They are not veterinary or medical advice, and they do not replace your teachers, textbooks, clinical supervisors or official guidance. They do not give drug doses. Clinical guidelines and legal rules change, and they differ between countries. For animal treatment, check the current national veterinary authority guidance and the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) standards. For zoonoses and food safety, also check World Health Organization (WHO) and national public health guidance. Never treat an animal from notes alone.

sections.heading: What veterinary medicine is
sections.text: Veterinary medicine is the science and practice of protecting animal health, welfare and production, and of protecting people from animal-linked disease. It covers companion animals, farm animals, horses, wildlife, aquatic animals and laboratory animals. A veterinarian diagnoses and treats disease, advises on herd health and nutrition, performs surgery, manages reproduction, inspects food, and helps control zoonoses, which are diseases that pass between animals and people. One Health is the idea that human, animal and environmental health are linked, so veterinarians work with doctors, ecologists and public health teams.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text: Veterinary degrees have different names and lengths. In Nigeria the usual award is the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM), and the Veterinary Council of Nigeria regulates registration. In the United Kingdom, awards include BVSc, BVMS and BVM&S. In the United States and Canada, the DVM is usually a four-year professional degree taken after preveterinary university study. Many programmes last five or six years, but this varies by country and institution. Check your own handbook and national veterinary council for the exact duration, award and licensing steps. Most degrees combine preclinical sciences, laboratory and disease sciences, clinical rotations and supervised practical work. Some schools use integrated organ-system teaching; others teach separate subjects.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with the profession and One Health, then the normal animal: cells, tissues and embryology; anatomy of the locomotor system, head and nervous system; anatomy of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis; physiology; biochemistry and molecular genetics; and biostatistics. These give the language for later work.

The core sciences follow: animal husbandry, behaviour and welfare; nutrition; microbiology; immunology; general pathology; pharmacology and toxicology. Then come clinical skills: examination and diagnostic reasoning, diagnostic imaging, anaesthesia and surgery. Clinical medicine covers farm animals and companion animals, infectious diseases, parasitology and theriogenology, the study of animal reproduction. Population and public health subjects include herd health and preventive medicine, veterinary public health, zoonoses and food safety, and ethics, law and professional practice.

Master’s level work adds advanced epidemiology and disease modelling, research methods and dissertation design, evidence-based veterinary medicine, and One Health with emerging zoonoses.

sections.heading: How to study
sections.text:
Start with normal structure and function, because disease makes sense only against that baseline. When you meet a sign, trace it back to anatomy, physiology or pathology. For example, link diarrhoea in a calf to fluid loss, acid-base change and dehydration, then to the likely causes and the questions you would ask.

Use active recall rather than rereading. Draw pathways, label anatomy from memory, and explain cases aloud. Space revision over weeks and mix topics. Practise clinical reasoning with case questions: list the problems, rank the likely causes, say what evidence would change your mind, and state the safety steps. In practical classes, learn handling, restraint and biosecurity properly. Read the current national guidance for notifiable diseases, which you must report by law, and for zoonoses. Keep notes on welfare and ethics, not only on diagnosis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often memorise disease lists without mechanisms, so they cannot reason through a new case. Others jump to a diagnosis and stop collecting evidence, which is premature closure. Some forget the herd or household context, or ignore cost, welfare and available resources. In examinations, candidates may miss urgent safety steps, fail to explain terms, or quote one country’s rule as universal.

Another mistake is to treat notes as a clinical manual. These pages cannot assess an animal or a person. Ask a qualified veterinarian, and follow local law and current official guidance.

keyPoints: Veterinary medicine protects animal health and welfare and also protects people from zoonoses.
One Health links human, animal and environmental health.
Degree names, lengths and licensing differ by country, so check your own handbook and veterinary council.
Teaching moves from normal structure and function to disease, clinical skills and population health.
Study by active recall, spaced revision and case reasoning, not by rereading.
These notes teach concepts only and are not veterinary advice or a source of drug doses.

en.title: Veterinary medicine as a profession: roles, history and One Health
en.short: Roles, history, One Health and professional limits in veterinary medicine.

sections.heading: Roles and scope
sections.text: Veterinary medicine protects animal health, human health and welfare. Veterinarians diagnose and treat disease, advise on herd health, perform surgery and certify animals and food. They also work in public health, food safety, research, teaching, policy and conservation. Scope varies by country: national law defines who may examine animals, prescribe medicines, operate or sign certificates. Veterinary nurses and technicians often carry out defined tasks under supervision. A veterinarian may see links between a sick herd, a farm family and local food.

sections.heading: How the profession grew
sections.text: Animal healing is ancient, but the modern profession took shape in Europe in the eighteenth century, when formal veterinary schools were founded. Early work focused on horses and farm animals, especially in wars and disease outbreaks. Knowledge of infectious disease, pathology and nutrition grew, and veterinarians took roles in meat inspection, laboratory diagnosis and disease control. Governments later established veterinary services, and universities in Africa and elsewhere trained local graduates. Regulators now set entry standards, codes of conduct and continuing education.

sections.heading: One Health
sections.text: One Health links human, animal and environmental health and needs joint action. It is not one law or programme. It brings veterinarians together with doctors, ecologists, farmers and other sectors. Examples include rabies control, food safety, antimicrobial resistance and zoonoses, diseases that pass from animals to people. In a farming district, milk from cows with mastitis may enter the food chain if hygiene and testing are weak. A veterinarian, public health officer and farmer can improve milking hygiene, treatment and monitoring. The aim is prevention and shared information, not blame.

sections.heading: Learning to practise
sections.text: Professional identity grows from knowledge, honesty and service. Good communication means plain language, listening, explaining uncertainty, obtaining consent and recording advice. Ask about housing, feed and work. Students must know their limits: under supervision you may take a history and perform permitted tasks, but not diagnose, treat or prescribe independently, or give drug doses. When unsure, say so and refer. Ethics, welfare and law guide decisions.

keyPoints: Veterinary medicine serves animal health, human health and animal welfare.
The scope of practice is set by national law and varies between countries.
The modern profession grew from eighteenth-century European veterinary schools and later spread through universities and government services.
One Health means human, animal and environmental health are linked and need joint action.
Good communication with owners uses plain language, consent and clear records.
Students must work within supervision and must not diagnose, treat or prescribe independently.

en.title: Cells, tissues and embryology
en.short: Cell organelles, the four animal tissues, germ layers and organ formation, and developmental defects.

sections.heading: Cell structure
sections.text: The cell is the basic unit of the animal body. A plasma membrane controls what enters and leaves. The nucleus holds DNA and directs protein synthesis. Mitochondria produce most ATP, the cell’s energy currency. Ribosomes make proteins. Endoplasmic reticulum folds proteins and makes lipids. The Golgi apparatus sorts and packages proteins. Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes. The cytoskeleton gives shape and movement. Cell function follows structure: muscle cells are packed with contractile proteins, and absorptive gut cells have microvilli. Histology is the study of tissues by microscopy.

sections.heading: Four basic tissues
sections.text: Animal tissues are grouped into four types. Epithelium covers surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands. Its cells sit close together with little matrix. Connective tissue supports and connects. It has cells such as fibroblasts and an extracellular matrix of fibres and ground substance. Examples include loose and dense connective tissue, cartilage, bone and blood. Muscle tissue contracts. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary, cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary, and smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary. Nervous tissue conducts electrical signals. Neurons have dendrites, a cell body and an axon, and glial cells support them. Tissues combine into organs. The intestine, for example, has epithelium, connective tissue, smooth muscle and nerves.

sections.heading: Embryonic development
sections.text: Development begins with fertilisation, forming a zygote. Cleavage divides it into smaller cells, forming a morula and then, in mammals, a blastocyst. Gastrulation rearranges cells into three germ layers. Ectoderm forms skin epidermis and nervous system. Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood, kidneys and reproductive organs. Endoderm lines the gut and forms liver, pancreas and lung lining. Neurulation forms the neural tube, which becomes brain and spinal cord. Organogenesis builds organs through division, movement, differentiation and programmed cell death. Teratogens are agents that disturb development, especially in critical periods. A calf with a ventricular septal defect has a hole between the ventricles. The septum normally separates the ventricles; incomplete formation leaves a shunt. Histology and embryology link normal structure to such defects.

keyPoints: The cell is the basic unit; organelles carry out specific functions.
The four basic animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Epithelium covers and lines; connective tissue supports; muscle contracts; nervous tissue signals.
Gastrulation forms ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, which give rise to the organs.
Neurulation forms the neural tube, the precursor of brain and spinal cord.
Histology and embryology explain normal structure and help explain defects such as ventricular septal defect.

en.title: Veterinary anatomy: locomotor system, head and nervous system
en.short: Bones, joints, muscles, skull, teeth, sense organs and the nervous system, with species differences.

sections.heading: Bones and joints
sections.text:
The skeleton has an axial part (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and an appendicular part (limbs and girdles). Bone is living tissue: hard cortical bone outside, spongy cancellous bone inside, covered by periosteum.

Fibrous and cartilaginous joints move little; synovial joints, such as the elbow and stifle, have cartilage, a capsule and synovial fluid. Learn where each joint lies under the skin: swelling there is a clinical sign.

sections.heading: Muscles and limbs
sections.text:
Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary. It attaches to bone by tendon: origin is the fixed end, insertion the moving end. Posture differs by species: horses are unguligrade (on one digit), cattle, sheep and pigs are cloven-hoofed (two digits), dogs and cats are digitigrade (on their toes).

Vertebral counts differ: dogs and cats usually have 13 thoracic and 7 lumbar vertebrae, horses 18 thoracic and 6 lumbar. Case: a dog lame on one forelimb may have pain at the shoulder joint or biceps tendon.

sections.heading: Skull, teeth and senses
sections.text:
The skull has a cranial part around the brain and a facial part. Teeth are incisors, canines, premolars and molars. The dog has 42 permanent teeth and the cat 30; ruminants have no upper incisors and press food against a dental pad.

The eye has a nictitating membrane (third eyelid), and dogs and cats have a tapetum lucidum, a reflective layer for dim light. The ear has a pinna, tympanic membrane, ossicles and inner ear.

sections.heading: Nervous system
sections.text:
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the cranial nerves, spinal nerves and autonomic nerves. Three meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia) surround the CNS in cerebrospinal fluid.

Birds differ: the spinal cord fills the vertebral canal, the cerebral hemispheres are smooth, and many bones are fused, such as the synsacrum and tarsometatarsus, with some bones air-filled. Surface landmarks guide safe work: the jugular groove for venepuncture, and the lumbosacral space in the dog or sacrococcygeal space in the cow for epidural injection. Check current guidance.

keyPoints: The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; the appendicular skeleton is the limbs and girdles.
Synovial joints have cartilage, a capsule and synovial fluid; fibrous and cartilaginous joints move little.
Muscle origin is the fixed attachment and insertion the moving one; horses are unguligrade, dogs and cats digitigrade.
Dental formulae differ: dog 42 permanent teeth, cat 30, and ruminants have no upper incisors.
The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, wrapped by three meninges; the PNS is the cranial, spinal and autonomic nerves.
Birds have fused bones such as the synsacrum and tarsometatarsus, and a spinal cord that fills the vertebral canal.

en.title: Veterinary anatomy: thorax, abdomen and pelvis
en.short: Thoracic, abdominal and pelvic organs, their vessels and nerves, and species differences.

sections.heading: Thorax
sections.text: The thorax is the chest cavity, bounded by ribs, sternum and spine and closed behind by the diaphragm. The mediastinum divides it and holds the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus; the lungs lie each side. The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm, the vagus and sympathetic trunk run in the mediastinum, and intercostal nerves supply the chest wall. In dogs and cats the heart lies low and left, so sounds are heard best on the left. In cattle and horses it is more central. Auscultation and percussion are the main examinations; thoracocentesis sites differ by species.

sections.heading: Abdomen
sections.text: The abdomen is bounded by abdominal muscles, spine and pelvis, with the diaphragm in front, and lined by peritoneum. Mesentery suspends intestine; omentum covers stomach. Topography is an organ’s position relative to landmarks. The stomach, intestines, liver, spleen, pancreas and kidneys lie here. Blood comes from the coeliac, cranial mesenteric and caudal mesenteric arteries; the portal vein drains the gut to the liver. Vagus is parasympathetic; sympathetic fibres come from coeliac and cranial mesenteric ganglia. In ruminants the rumen fills the left flank, so rumenotomy uses a left flank incision. In horses the large colon is large and mobile, explaining displacement. A cow with a swollen left flank and poor appetite likely has a rumen problem; the left flank approach reaches it safely.

sections.heading: Pelvis
sections.text: The pelvis is the bony ring formed by the hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis) and the sacrum, containing rectum, bladder, urethra and reproductive organs. The internal pudendal artery and pudendal nerve supply the perineum and external genitalia; the pelvic plexus supplies pelvic organs. In the bitch the uterus lies in the abdomen, not the pelvis. Rectal palpation in cow and mare is possible because the rectum is roomy and the arm can reach through the pelvic inlet; it is used to feel uterus and ovaries. Dystocia, difficult birth, is assessed by pelvic size and fetal position.

keyPoints: The diaphragm closes the thorax; the mediastinum holds the heart and great vessels.
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; intercostal nerves supply the chest wall.
Peritoneum lines the abdomen; mesentery and omentum suspend organs.
Coeliac, cranial mesenteric and caudal mesenteric arteries supply the gut; the portal vein drains it.
The rumen fills the left flank in ruminants, guiding a left flank surgical approach.
In the bitch the uterus is abdominal, so it is not reached through the pelvis.

en.title: Physiology: homeostasis, blood and body fluids
en.short: Homeostasis, membrane transport, body fluids, blood composition, haemostasis and acid-base basics.

sections.heading: Homeostasis and transport
sections.text: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable around a set point despite change. Negative feedback detects a deviation, a control centre responds, and an effector corrects it. For example, dehydration raises plasma osmotic pressure, and thirst drives drinking while antidiuretic hormone reduces water loss. Cell membranes are selectively permeable. Passive transport moves substances down a gradient by diffusion or osmosis; facilitated diffusion uses channels or carriers without energy. Active transport uses ATP to move ions against a gradient. Fluid shifts and electrolyte loss impair cell function.

sections.heading: Fluid compartments
sections.text: Body water is divided into intracellular fluid inside cells and extracellular fluid outside. Extracellular fluid includes interstitial fluid around cells and plasma in vessels. Water moves between compartments by osmosis, while capillary filtration and reabsorption depend on hydrostatic pressure (blood pressure) and oncotic pressure (from plasma proteins). In vomiting, diarrhoea or blood loss, extracellular fluid falls, plasma volume may drop, and perfusion and kidney function suffer. Fluid needs are assessed clinically, not by one fixed rule.

sections.heading: Blood and haemostasis
sections.text: Blood is plasma plus cells: red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells defend the body, and platelets help clot. Plasma contains water, electrolytes, proteins, nutrients and hormones. Haemostasis stops bleeding in stages: vascular constriction, platelet plug formation, coagulation producing fibrin, then fibrinolysis removes the clot. Disorders include anaemia (low red cells), low platelets and clotting failure. In animals, haemorrhage, tick-borne disease and poisoning can disturb these systems. Pallor, petechiae (pinpoint skin bleeds) or prolonged bleeding need veterinary assessment.

sections.heading: Acid-base basics
sections.text: Acid-base balance keeps blood pH within a narrow range. pH expresses hydrogen ion concentration; bicarbonate is the main extracellular buffer that resists pH change. The lungs remove carbon dioxide, an acid, while the kidneys excrete hydrogen ions and reabsorb bicarbonate. Respiratory or metabolic disturbances cause acidosis or alkalosis, and compensation reduces the change. For example, a calf with severe diarrhoea may lose bicarbonate and develop metabolic acidosis. Diagnosis uses history, examination and blood gas or bicarbonate measurement, interpreted with current laboratory and national guidance.

keyPoints: Homeostasis uses negative feedback to keep internal conditions near a set point.
Passive transport follows gradients; active transport uses ATP to move substances against them.
Body water is in intracellular and extracellular compartments, and plasma is part of extracellular fluid.
Blood is plasma plus red cells, white cells and platelets; haemostasis forms a platelet plug and fibrin clot.
pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration, and bicarbonate buffers extracellular fluid.
Fluid loss, anaemia and clotting failure matter because they reduce perfusion, oxygen delivery or haemostasis.

en.title: Physiology: heart, lungs, kidneys and acid-base balance
en.short: How the heart, lungs and kidneys work together to control blood pressure, gases, water and acid-base balance.

sections.heading: Cardiac cycle and blood pressure
sections.text: The cardiac cycle is one heartbeat: diastole (filling) then systole (ejection). Stroke volume (SV) is blood ejected per beat; heart rate (HR) is beats per minute. Cardiac output (CO) is HR × SV. Blood pressure (BP) is CO × total peripheral resistance, the sum of arteriolar tone. Baroreceptors and hormones adjust both. For example, HR 120 beats/min × SV 20 mL = 2,400 mL/min, or 2.4 L/min.

sections.heading: Lungs: mechanics and gas exchange
sections.text: Lung mechanics move air by pressure gradients. Inspiration expands the chest; alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Compliance is stretchability; surfactant lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Gas exchange is diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar-capillary membrane, driven by partial pressure gradients. Ventilation must match blood flow. In mammals the diaphragm drives breathing; birds have a flow-through lung and air sacs.

sections.heading: Kidneys: filtration and reabsorption
sections.text: Renal filtration begins in the glomerulus, where blood pressure pushes water and small solutes into Bowman’s capsule; cells and large proteins stay in blood. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume filtered per minute. Tubular reabsorption returns useful substances: glucose and amino acids, most sodium and water, and bicarbonate. Secretion adds hydrogen ions, potassium and some drugs. Hormones regulate water and electrolytes: antidiuretic hormone (ADH) conserves water, aldosterone conserves sodium, and atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium loss.

sections.heading: Integration in exercise and disease
sections.text: Acid-base balance depends on lungs and kidneys. Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid; ventilation removes CO2. The kidneys reabsorb bicarbonate and excrete hydrogen ions. During exercise, muscles increase oxygen use and CO2 and acid production; heart rate and ventilation rise, and the kidneys excrete the extra acid over the following hours. Heat stress shifts blood to skin for cooling and causes water and electrolyte loss, so urine becomes concentrated. Disease can break the integration: heart failure causes fluid retention, lung disease causes low oxygen, and kidney disease causes acid and potassium retention. Species and individual values vary; use current veterinary references.

keyPoints: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; blood pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.
Lung mechanics depend on pressure gradients, compliance and surfactant; gas exchange depends on partial pressure gradients and matching ventilation to blood flow.
Glomerular filtration is pressure-driven; tubular reabsorption reclaims water, glucose, sodium and bicarbonate.
ADH conserves water, aldosterone conserves sodium, and the kidneys excrete hydrogen ions to correct acidosis.
During exercise and heat stress, the heart, lungs and kidneys adjust together; disease disrupts this integration.
Species differ, especially in lung structure and normal values; check current veterinary references.

en.title: Physiology: digestion, metabolism, endocrine and reproductive physiology
en.short: How animals digest feed, use energy and protein, and control hormones and reproduction.

sections.heading: Digestion and absorption
sections.text:
Digestion breaks feed into small molecules that cross the gut wall. Monogastric animals such as pigs and dogs digest mainly by enzymes: starch becomes glucose, protein becomes amino acids, fat becomes fatty acids, and absorption happens in the small intestine.

Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have four stomach chambers: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Rumen microbes ferment fibre into volatile fatty acids (VFAs), mainly acetate, propionate and butyrate, which the animal absorbs and burns for energy. The microbes also supply microbial protein and B vitamins. Rumen pH and the microbe population change with diet.

sections.heading: Energy and protein metabolism
sections.text:
Energy is measured in stages. Gross energy is total energy in the feed. Digestible energy (DE) is what is absorbed. Metabolisable energy (ME) subtracts losses in urine and gas. Cells use ATP as their energy currency.

Protein is built from amino acids. Essential amino acids must come from the diet. Ruminants depend on microbial protein, while monogastrics need good dietary amino acid balance. Nitrogen balance compares nitrogen eaten with nitrogen lost.

Worked example: a feed has 18 MJ/kg gross energy, 70 per cent digestible, and 80 per cent of DE is metabolisable.
DE = 18 × 0.70 = 12.6 MJ/kg
ME = 12.6 × 0.80 = 10.08 MJ/kg

sections.heading: Endocrine glands and hormones
sections.text: Hormones are chemical messengers released into the blood that act on target cells with matching receptors. Peptide hormones act at the cell surface through second messengers. Steroid hormones enter the cell and change gene activity. Most axes work by negative feedback: the hypothalamus releases a hormone, the anterior pituitary releases a trophic hormone, and the target gland releases its hormone, which then restrains the earlier steps. Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it.

sections.heading: Reproductive cycle
sections.text:
The female cycle has stages: proestrus, oestrus (heat), metoestrus and dioestrus, with anoestrus as a resting phase. GnRH from the hypothalamus drives FSH and LH from the pituitary. FSH grows follicles, oestrogen peaks at heat, LH triggers ovulation, and progesterone from the corpus luteum supports pregnancy. Prostaglandin F2α from the uterus ends the corpus luteum.

Patterns differ by species: sheep and horses are seasonally polyoestrous, dogs are monoestrous, and cats and rabbits ovulate after mating. In males, spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules, testosterone comes from Leydig cells, and Sertoli cells support developing sperm. Clinical reproduction is covered in theriogenology.

keyPoints: Monogastrics digest mainly by enzymes; ruminants rely on microbial fermentation.
Rumen microbes produce volatile fatty acids and microbial protein.
DE = gross energy × digestibility; ME = DE × metabolisable fraction.
Hormones act on target cells with receptors; most axes use negative feedback.
Oestrus is the heat phase; LH triggers ovulation and progesterone maintains pregnancy.
Reproductive patterns differ by species, so breeding plans must match the species.

en.title: Veterinary biochemistry and molecular genetics
en.short: Animal biomolecules, enzymes, energy metabolism, genes, inheritance, mutation and molecular tools.

sections.heading: Biomolecules and enzymes
sections.text: Biomolecules are the molecules of life. Carbohydrates supply energy, lipids form membranes and store energy, proteins build tissues and act as enzymes, and nucleic acids store genetic information. Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy. Each enzyme usually acts on a specific substrate. Activity depends on temperature, pH and cofactors such as metal ions or coenzymes. Blood enzyme tests can show organ damage in animals.

sections.heading: Energy metabolism
sections.text: Metabolism is the sum of reactions. Catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy; anabolism builds molecules and uses energy. ATP is the cell’s main energy currency. Animals make ATP by oxidising glucose, fatty acids and amino acids. Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm. The Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria release more ATP. When oxygen is low, glycolysis can produce lactate. Energy supply must match demand; negative energy balance in dairy cows can cause ketosis.

sections.heading: Genes and inheritance
sections.text: DNA is a double helix. A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a product, usually a protein. Replication copies DNA before cell division. Transcription makes RNA from DNA, and translation makes protein from messenger RNA. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene. Genotype is the allele pair; phenotype is the observable trait. In a simple recessive disorder, carriers are Aa and affected animals are aa. A mating of two carriers, Aa × Aa, gives offspring AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Thus 1 in 4 offspring, 25%, is expected to be affected.

sections.heading: Mutation and molecular tools
sections.text: A mutation is a change in DNA sequence. Point mutations may be silent, missense or nonsense. Insertions or deletions can shift the reading frame. Mutations may be inherited or acquired in body cells. They create genetic variation and can cause disease or affect production traits. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies a chosen DNA segment. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size. DNA sequencing reads the base order. These tools support parentage testing, carrier screening and breeding selection. Interpret results with current laboratory and national guidance.

keyPoints: Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy and are specific to substrates.
ATP is the main energy currency; glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation supply it.
DNA replication copies the genome; transcription makes RNA and translation makes protein.
Alleles are alternative gene forms; genotype is the pair and phenotype is the observable trait.
For a recessive allele, Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 1 in 4 offspring is expected affected.
PCR, gel electrophoresis and DNA sequencing detect mutations and support parentage testing and breeding selection.

en.title: Biostatistics and data literacy in veterinary science
en.short: Describing data, sampling, study designs, tests, intervals and critical reading of veterinary research.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Biostatistics helps you judge whether a veterinary finding is real and important. A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the part you study. Random sampling gives every animal a known chance of selection and reduces bias. Describe data with the mean (average) and standard deviation (SD), which measures spread, or with the median and range when data are skewed. Probability is the chance of an event.

Worked example: five dog weights are 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18 kg. Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 kg. Deviations from the mean are −4, −2, 0, 2 and 4; their squares sum to 40. Sample variance = 40 ÷ (5 − 1) = 10, so SD = √10 ≈ 3.16 kg.

sections.heading: Designs and tests
sections.text:
Common designs include cross-sectional surveys, cohort studies, case-control studies and randomised controlled trials (RCTs). A cohort follows exposed and unexposed animals forward. A case-control study compares affected and unaffected animals backward. An RCT assigns treatment at random, so it best supports cause. Observational studies can show association, not proof of causation.

A hypothesis test asks whether data fit a null hypothesis, usually no difference. The p value is the probability of results at least as extreme if the null is true; it is not the probability the null is true. A 95% confidence interval (CI) is a range of plausible values; for a large sample it is often mean ± 1.96 × standard error (SE), where SE = SD ÷ √n. A CI gives the size and precision of an effect.

sections.heading: Reading critically
sections.text: Read tables and graphs by checking labels, units, scales and sample size. A cut axis can exaggerate a small change. Ask if groups were comparable, confounding was controlled, and the result applies to your animals. Statistical significance is not clinical importance: a tiny difference can be significant in a large study. Do not overstate a single study; look for replication and current national veterinary or World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) guidance.

keyPoints: A sample describes a population; random sampling reduces selection bias.
Mean and SD summarise symmetric data; median and range suit skewed data.
Cohort studies follow forward, case-control studies compare backward, and RCTs randomise treatment.
A p value is the probability of data at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the null is true.
SE = SD ÷ √n; a large-sample 95% CI is often mean ± 1.96 × SE.
Association is not causation, and statistical significance is not clinical importance.

en.title: Animal husbandry, behaviour and welfare
en.short: Production and housing systems, handling, normal behaviour and welfare assessment for farm and companion animals.

sections.heading: Husbandry and housing
sections.text: Husbandry is the day-to-day care and management of animals: feeding, water, shelter, hygiene, breeding and records. Production systems range from extensive, with low inputs and grazing over large areas, through semi-intensive, to intensive, with high stocking rates and controlled housing. Each has welfare risks. Extensive systems may expose animals to heat, parasites and predators; intensive systems may cause crowding, poor air quality and foot problems. Housing must meet species needs for space, ventilation, dry lying areas, shade and social contact. Dogs and cats need space, enrichment and escape from fear-provoking sights and sounds.

sections.heading: Behaviour and handling
sections.text: Normal behaviour includes feeding, resting, social interaction, grooming, exploration and, in some species, grazing or rooting. Learn each species’ normal pattern so changes such as reduced feeding, isolation or stereotypy, repeated purposeless movement, are noticed early. Handling and restraint should be calm, planned and minimal. Understand the flight zone, the distance at which an animal moves away, and use gentle pressure to move cattle. Restraint may be manual or use a crush or head gate; it must fit the animal and never rely on pain. In a smallholder dairy in Kenya, Wanjiku moves cows to milking quietly, avoiding shouting. Cows enter calmly, injuries fall and milk let-down improves.

sections.heading: Welfare assessment
sections.text: Animal welfare is the state of an animal as it copes with its environment. The Five Freedoms are a framework: freedom from hunger and thirst, discomfort, pain injury or disease, and fear or distress, plus freedom to express normal behaviour. Assessment combines resource-based measures, such as space, water and ventilation, with animal-based measures, such as lameness, wounds, body condition and behaviour. Records of illness and mortality add context. Poor husbandry causes stress, which can reduce growth and fertility and increase susceptibility to disease. Injuries come from slippery floors, sharp edges and rough restraint. Local laws and welfare standards vary by country; check agriculture or veterinary authority guidance and the standards of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH).

keyPoints: Husbandry and housing must match species needs for space, ventilation, dry lying areas, shade and social contact.
Extensive and intensive systems each carry welfare risks, including heat, parasites, crowding and poor air quality.
Learn normal behaviour for each species so changes such as reduced feeding or stereotypy are noticed early.
Calm, minimal handling uses the flight zone and well-fitting restraint, never pain.
Welfare assessment combines resource-based and animal-based measures with records of illness and mortality.
Local welfare laws and standards vary by country; check national veterinary or agriculture authority guidance and WOAH standards.

en.title: Animal nutrition and ration formulation
en.short: Nutrient needs, feedstuffs, digestion and ration formulation for farm and companion animals.

sections.heading: Nutrient needs
sections.text: Animals need water, energy, protein, minerals and vitamins. Requirements are stated as amounts per day or as concentrations in dry matter (DM), the feed left after water is removed. Crude protein (CP) is nitrogen × 6.25; it estimates protein but not amino acid balance. Feeding standards estimate needs as maintenance plus production. Maintenance keeps the animal alive; growth adds tissue, pregnancy adds fetal and placental growth, and lactation adds milk. Late pregnancy and lactation are especially demanding. Use current tables; values vary by species, weight, age and production level.

sections.heading: Feedstuffs and digestion
sections.text: Feedstuffs include forages (grass, hay, silage), concentrates (cereals, oilseed meals), by-products and supplements. Ruminants digest fibre by microbial fermentation in the rumen, producing volatile fatty acids. Pigs are monogastric: enzymes digest starch and protein, with some hindgut fermentation. Poultry have a crop, gizzard and short hindgut; they digest fibre poorly. Dogs are omnivorous; cats are carnivorous and need nutrients such as taurine and preformed vitamin A in the diet. Diet form and processing affect intake and digestibility.

sections.heading: Ration formulation
sections.text: Ration formulation matches feed amounts to requirements without excess. A simple example uses maize at 9% CP and soybean meal at 48% CP, on a DM basis. If a growing pig diet targets 18% CP, let x be the soybean meal fraction: 0.48x + 0.09(1 − x) = 0.18. Then 0.39x = 0.09, so x = 0.23. The mix is about 23% soybean meal and 77% maize. Check: 0.23 × 48 = 11.04 and 0.77 × 9 = 6.93, giving 17.97, about 18% CP. This only balances protein; energy, minerals, vitamins and amino acids must also be checked.

sections.heading: Quality and safety
sections.text: Feed quality depends on DM, digestibility, palatability and contaminants. Energy or protein deficiency reduces growth, milk and fertility; copper, selenium and iodine deficiencies occur. Excess selenium, salt or nitrate can poison. Mycotoxins like aflatoxin damage liver and immunity. Store dry, test suspect batches, and follow national feed law and guidance.

keyPoints: Requirements are water, energy, protein, minerals and vitamins, estimated as maintenance plus production.
Ruminants ferment fibre in the rumen; pigs and poultry are monogastric; cats need taurine and preformed vitamin A.
Crude protein = nitrogen × 6.25, but amino acid balance also matters.
For two feeds, solve 0.48x + 0.09(1 − x) = 0.18 to find the soybean meal fraction in an 18% CP mix.
Deficiencies reduce growth, milk and fertility; excess selenium, salt or nitrate can poison.
Feed quality and safety depend on storage, contaminant testing and national feed law, which varies by country.

en.title: Veterinary microbiology
en.short: Animal pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, prions), laboratory diagnosis, sterilisation and resistance.

sections.heading: Pathogen classes
sections.text: Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes with a peptidoglycan cell wall. They divide by binary fission, and in culture they pass through lag, log, stationary and death phases. Most grow on agar, which allows colony counting and sensitivity testing. Viruses are much smaller: a nucleic acid core, DNA or RNA, inside a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope. They replicate only inside living cells, so laboratories use cell culture, embryonated eggs or animals. Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin walls; moulds form branching hyphae and yeasts bud. Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid.

sections.heading: Transmission
sections.text: Pathogens spread by direct contact, droplets and aerosol, the faecal-oral route, contaminated objects (fomites), vectors such as ticks, and vertically from dam to offspring. Many are zoonotic, meaning they pass from animals to people. Prions spread mainly when animals eat infected tissue. The route shapes control: aerosol spread responds to ventilation and stocking density, while faecal-oral spread responds to hygiene and water quality.

sections.heading: Diagnosis in the laboratory
sections.text: Tunde keeps 400 laying hens near Abeokuta, Nigeria. Sudden deaths and greenish diarrhoea appear. He sends swabs and spleen to a laboratory. RT-PCR detects Newcastle disease virus RNA. Culture on selective agar with biochemical tests screens for Salmonella. Paired blood samples show a rising antibody titre. Fungi are seen on potassium hydroxide microscopy and grown on Sabouraud agar. Prions cannot be cultured or found by PCR; diagnosis uses brain histopathology and immunohistochemistry for the abnormal protein.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and resistance
sections.text: Sterilisation kills all microbes, including spores. Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects but may spare spores, and antisepsis means applying agents to living tissue. Autoclaving uses steam under pressure, typically 121 °C for 15 minutes. Organic dirt blunts disinfectants, so clean surfaces first. Biosecurity means quarantine, traffic control, all-in/all-out stocking and pest control. Antimicrobial resistance arises through drug-destroying enzymes, efflux pumps, target changes and gene transfer on plasmids. Prudent-use rules differ by country; check the national regulator and WOAH (World Organisation for Animal Health) guidance.

keyPoints: Bacteria grow by binary fission through lag, log, stationary and death phases.
Viruses need living cells; they cannot grow on plain agar.
Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid, so PCR and culture fail.
Sterilisation kills spores; disinfection may not, so clean organic matter away first.
Resistance spreads between bacteria on plasmids as well as by mutation.
Prudent antimicrobial rules vary by country; check the national regulator and WOAH.

en.title: Veterinary immunology
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, vaccination and immune disease in animals.

sections.heading: Innate and adaptive immunity
sections.text: Immunity is the body’s ability to resist infection. Innate immunity acts at once and is not specific. It includes skin and mucous membranes, phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages, complement proteins and inflammation. Adaptive immunity is slower and specific. Lymphocytes carry it: B cells make antibodies, and T cells help B cells or kill infected cells. Memory cells make a second response faster and stronger. An antigen is any molecule the immune system recognises. An antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds an antigen.

sections.heading: Antibodies and infection
sections.text: After infection, innate defences slow the pathogen while lymphocytes expand. IgM appears first, then IgG; IgA protects surfaces, IgE drives allergy and IgD is mainly a B cell receptor. T cells are needed for viruses and intracellular bacteria because antibodies cannot reach inside cells. Memory gives protection, but some pathogens evade immunity by changing antigens or suppressing responses. In young animals, passive immunity comes from colostrum, the first milk, which contains antibodies. A calf with poor colostrum intake is at higher risk of infection.

sections.heading: Vaccination principles
sections.text: A vaccine presents antigens in a safe form to produce active immunity and memory without causing disease. Types include live attenuated, killed, subunit and toxoid (inactivated toxin) vaccines. Adjuvants strengthen the response. Maternal antibodies can block some vaccines in young animals, so timing matters. Vaccines are tested in laboratory studies, challenge trials and field trials for safety, potency and efficacy, then licensed by national regulators under international animal health standards. At herd level, use depends on storage, coverage, records and surveillance. A farm in Nakuru, Kenya, records calf colostrum intake and heifer vaccination coverage, then reviews disease rates with its veterinarian. Check national guidance.

sections.heading: Immune disease
sections.text: Immunodeficiency is a failure of defence, causing repeated infections; it may be inherited or secondary to malnutrition, infection or stress. Allergy is a harmful response to a harmless antigen, such as atopy (environmental allergy) or food allergy. Autoimmune disease is immune attack on self, as in immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia in dogs.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is slower, specific and leaves memory.
B cells make antibodies; T cells help B cells or kill infected cells.
IgM appears early, IgG later; IgA protects surfaces and IgE drives allergy.
Colostrum gives passive immunity, so poor intake raises infection risk in young animals.
Vaccines produce active immunity and memory; testing checks safety, potency and efficacy before licensing.
Immunodeficiency, allergy and autoimmune disease all reflect immune dysfunction, not simply infection.

en.title: General pathology: mechanisms of disease in animals
en.short: How animal cells and tissues respond to injury, inflammation, repair, circulatory disturbance and cancer.

sections.heading: Cell injury and death
sections.text:
Pathology links causes to tissue changes and clinical signs. Cell injury may be reversible, with swelling, or irreversible, usually necrosis. Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death that releases contents and causes inflammation. Patterns suggest causes: coagulative necrosis in infarcts, liquefactive in brain, caseous in tuberculosis, fat necrosis after trauma.

Apoptosis is programmed death without inflammation. Species vary: cattle often form caseous granulomas in tuberculosis; dogs often form liquefactive abscesses.

sections.heading: Inflammation and infection
sections.text:
Acute inflammation is the first response to injury or infection. Vessels widen and leak, causing redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages. Mediators include histamine, prostaglandins and cytokines.

Chronic inflammation involves macrophages and lymphocytes and may form granulomas, as in tuberculosis and schistosomiasis. Infection also causes fever, lethargy and raised acute phase proteins. Pus is dead neutrophils, fluid and debris. These changes explain signs such as a painful abscess or weight loss in chronic disease.

sections.heading: Repair and circulation
sections.text:
Repair occurs by regeneration or fibrosis. Granulation tissue, new vessels and fibroblasts, fills wounds. First intention healing occurs in clean surgical wounds; second intention in open wounds. Circulatory disturbances include hyperaemia, congestion, haemorrhage, oedema, thrombosis, embolism and infarction.

A thrombus is a clot inside a vessel; an embolus travels and blocks elsewhere; an infarct is tissue death from lost blood supply. Virchow triad names vessel injury, slow flow and increased clotting tendency. These cause swelling, pain, pallor or organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: Neoplasia and samples
sections.text:
Neoplasia is abnormal growth that continues without control. Benign tumours stay local; malignant tumours invade and metastasise. Carcinomas arise from epithelium; sarcomas from connective tissue. Grade describes cell abnormality; stage describes spread. Examples: canine mast cell tumour, bovine lymphoma, feline injection site sarcoma.

Tissue samples are described by site, size, colour, margins, distribution and microscopic features such as necrosis, inflammation and cell type. A biopsy or postmortem report links these findings to mechanisms and clinical signs. Confirm with the pathologist and current guidance; this is education, not clinical advice.

keyPoints: Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death with inflammation; apoptosis is programmed and non-inflammatory.
Acute inflammation causes redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function; neutrophils arrive first.
Chronic inflammation involves macrophages and lymphocytes and may form granulomas.
Repair is by regeneration or fibrosis; granulation tissue fills wounds.
Virchow triad: vessel injury, slow flow and increased clotting tendency.
Neoplasia is uncontrolled growth; grade describes cells and stage describes spread.

en.title: Veterinary pharmacology and toxicology
en.short: Pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, drug classes and routes, species differences, toxicology and withdrawal periods.

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
sections.text: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME). Absorption depends on route and species. Distribution depends on blood flow, fat and protein binding. Metabolism often happens in the liver; excretion mainly by kidney or bile. Half-life is the time for plasma concentration to fall by half. After four half-lives about 6.25% remains, because (1/2)^4 = 1/16. This helps explain dosing intervals, but actual doses come from current veterinary formularies.

sections.heading: Pharmacodynamics and routes
sections.text: Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body. Most drugs act on receptors, enzymes or ion channels. An agonist activates a receptor; an antagonist blocks it. The therapeutic index compares harmful and useful doses: a narrow index needs careful monitoring. Drug classes include antimicrobials, anthelmintics, NSAIDs, anaesthetics and vaccines. Routes include oral, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, topical, inhalation and intramammary. Species differences matter: cats metabolise some drugs slowly because of limited glucuronidation; some dog breeds carry the MDR1 mutation and are sensitive to certain drugs; ruminant rumen microbes alter oral drugs; birds have high metabolic rates.

sections.heading: Toxicology
sections.text: Toxicology studies poisons. Harm depends on dose, route, species, age and duration. Some toxic plants in Africa include Lantana camara and Senecio species, which can damage the liver. Chemicals include pesticides, rodenticides and heavy metals. Diagnosis uses history, clinical signs, and sometimes laboratory tests. Treatment principles are removing exposure, supportive care and specific antidotes where available. Do not give drug doses here; follow current national guidance and poisons centre advice.

sections.heading: Withdrawal periods
sections.text: Withdrawal periods are waiting times after the last treatment before meat, milk, eggs or honey can be sold. They protect consumers from drug residues. They vary by drug, formulation, species, route and country, and are set by regulators. Always check the product label and current national rules. For example, a dairy farmer must discard milk for the stated period after treating a cow; the exact period cannot be assumed.

keyPoints: Pharmacokinetics is ADME; pharmacodynamics is the drug’s effect on the body.
After n half-lives, the fraction of drug remaining is (1/2)^n; four half-lives leave 6.25%.
Species differences in metabolism and anatomy change drug handling, so a drug safe in one species may be toxic in another.
Toxicology assesses dose, route, species and exposure; treatment starts by stopping exposure and giving supportive care.
Withdrawal periods protect food safety and vary by product, species and country; always check the current label and regulator.
Never assume a dose or withdrawal time; use current veterinary formularies and national guidance.

en.title: Clinical examination and diagnostic reasoning
en.short: History, safe restraint, physical examination and problem-based diagnosis in animals.

sections.heading: History and restraint
sections.text: Begin with signalment: species, breed, age, sex and reproductive status. Ask the owner, in their own words, about the main complaint, its onset and course, appetite, water intake, urine and faeces, behaviour, vaccination, deworming, diet, housing and other animals affected. A good history often suggests the likely body systems. Restraint must be safe for animal, handler and clinician. Use the least force needed, a species-appropriate method and quiet surroundings. Explain to the owner. Never restrain an animal in a way that compromises breathing or causes pain.

sections.heading: Physical examination
sections.text: Examine systematically and compare left with right: general demeanour, body condition, mucous membranes, hydration, temperature, pulse and respiration. Then examine each system, including lymph nodes, skin, eyes, ears, mouth, thorax, abdomen, limbs and nervous function. In cattle and horses, use auscultation and palpation per rectum only where trained. In small animals, handle gently and watch for pain or aggression. Record findings as normal or abnormal; do not rely on memory.

sections.heading: Problem-based reasoning
sections.text: Turn findings into a problem list, such as chronic weight loss or hindlimb lameness. For each problem, list differential diagnoses: common, dangerous and treatable causes first. Use history and examination to rank them. Basic tests include packed cell volume and total protein, blood smear, biochemistry, urinalysis, faecal examination and cytology. Interpret results against the laboratory’s species-specific reference interval, the range seen in healthy animals, because values differ with age, breed and method. A test rarely proves a diagnosis alone; its limits are described by sensitivity (how often it is positive in diseased animals) and specificity (how often it is negative in healthy ones). Example: Mrs Okafor’s goat is thin and has pale mucous membranes. Differential diagnoses include parasitism, chronic infection and malnutrition. A faecal egg count and packed cell volume help rank them, but a negative result does not exclude disease.

sections.heading: Referral and guidelines
sections.text: Refer when you lack equipment, expertise or confidence, when the animal is deteriorating, or when imaging, surgery or intensive care is needed. Telephone the referral centre first. Clinical guidelines, drug rules and notifiable disease lists vary by country; check current national veterinary authority guidance.

keyPoints: Start with signalment and a full history; it often points to the body system involved.
Use the least restraint needed and protect animal, handler and clinician.
Examine systematically and record normal and abnormal findings.
Build a problem list and rank differential diagnoses by commonness, danger and treatability.
Interpret laboratory results against species-specific reference intervals; one test rarely proves a diagnosis.
Refer when equipment, expertise or intensive care is lacking, and check current national guidance.

en.title: Diagnostic imaging in animals
en.short: Radiography, ultrasound, CT and MRI: principles, positioning, findings, safety and limits.

sections.heading: Principles and safety
sections.text:
Diagnostic imaging uses physical signals to show anatomy and disease without surgery. Radiography passes X-rays through tissue: bone and metal are radiopaque (white), gas is radiolucent (black). Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound; fluid is usually anechoic (black). CT reconstructs cross-sectional X-ray images, and MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves. Choose a method by tissue, size and safety.

Radiation safety follows ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable. Collimate the beam, use lead aprons and gloves, avoid holding animals in the beam, and monitor staff dose. National radiation rules differ; follow current law and local protocols. Sedation or anaesthesia must be authorised by a veterinarian.

sections.heading: Positioning and normal anatomy
sections.text: Good positioning gives diagnostic images and reduces repeats. In radiography, take at least two orthogonal views (at right angles), such as lateral and ventrodorsal, label the animal and side, and measure thickness for exposure. Use sandbags, ties and troughs; manual restraint only by trained staff, never in the primary beam. In ultrasound, clip hair, apply gel and use a consistent acoustic window. Learn normal silhouettes: bone cortex, heart and liver shape, kidney size, bladder and lung patterns. Compare with the opposite side and normal reference images.

sections.heading: Findings and limits
sections.text:
Describe findings systematically: site, size, shape, margin, number and effect on nearby tissue. Radiographs may show fractures, foreign bodies, free gas, effusion or loss of serosal detail (organs lose their crisp edges, often from fluid). Ultrasound may show free fluid, masses, altered echogenicity (tissue brightness), stones or intestinal layering. CT and MRI give cross-sectional detail but usually need sedation or general anaesthesia; MRI almost always needs general anaesthesia. Radiography has poor soft-tissue contrast and summation (overlapping shadows); ultrasound is operator dependent and blocked by gas or bone; CT uses more radiation; MRI is slow and costly. A normal image does not exclude disease.

A vomiting dog has abdominal radiographs showing reduced serosal detail and a gas-filled loop. Ultrasound finds a jejunal foreign body and free fluid. The findings guide surgery. Radiography gave an overview; ultrasound gave soft-tissue detail; neither replaced clinical examination.

keyPoints: Radiography uses X-rays; bone and metal are radiopaque, gas is radiolucent.
Ultrasound uses sound; fluid is usually anechoic and gas or bone blocks the beam.
Take at least two orthogonal radiographic views and label side; use safe restraint outside the primary beam.
Follow ALARA and national radiation law: collimate, shield, avoid hand holding in the beam and monitor dose.
Describe findings by site, size, shape, margin, number and effect on nearby tissue.
Each method has limits; a normal image does not exclude disease, so combine imaging with clinical examination.

en.title: Anaesthesia and surgery
en.short: Pre-anaesthetic assessment, monitoring, pain control, asepsis, instruments, wounds and common operations.

sections.heading: Pre-anaesthetic assessment
sections.text:
Pre-anaesthetic assessment means judging risk before anaesthesia. Take a history, examine the animal, and note age, weight, temperament, pregnancy, previous reactions and concurrent disease. Dehydration, shock, pain, heart or lung disease and kidney or liver disease increase risk. Stabilise the animal first when possible: treat dehydration, control severe pain and improve oxygen delivery. Record a risk category and plan anaesthesia and recovery.

Species and countries differ in drug availability and legal restrictions; check current national veterinary medicines rules.

sections.heading: Equipment and monitoring
sections.text:
Anaesthetic equipment includes the machine, vaporiser, breathing circuit, oxygen supply, endotracheal tubes and scavenging system. Check and leak-test the machine before use. Monitoring means watching depth of anaesthesia and vital signs: heart and respiratory rates, mucous membrane colour, capillary refill, pulse strength, temperature and reflexes. Pulse oximetry, capnography and blood pressure help, but hands-on observation remains essential.

Recovery is risky. Provide warmth and oxygen, and watch until the animal is awake and swallowing.

sections.heading: Asepsis and instruments
sections.text: Asepsis keeps microbes out of a surgical site. It includes sterile gowns, gloves, drapes and instruments, skin preparation, and limiting theatre traffic. Sterilisation kills all microbes; disinfection reduces them. Instruments have named uses: scalpel for cutting, scissors for dividing tissue, haemostats for clamping vessels, forceps for grasping, needle holders for suturing and retractors for exposure. Handle them safely and count them before and after surgery.

sections.heading: Wounds and procedures
sections.text:
Wound management starts with lavage and removal of dead tissue. Decide whether to close, leave open to heal, or use dressings. Contaminated wounds are often left open or drained. Common procedures include ovariohysterectomy, castration, caesarean section, wound repair and abscess drainage. For example, a bitch with pyometra needs fluids and pain relief before ovariohysterectomy; asepsis and monitoring continue.

Pain control uses pre-emptive, multimodal analgesia: local blocks, opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs where available. Assess pain with a scale and reassess. Guidelines change, so follow current national guidance.

keyPoints: Pre-anaesthetic assessment identifies risk and allows stabilisation before anaesthesia.
Check anaesthetic equipment and monitor vital signs and depth throughout, including recovery.
Asepsis depends on sterile equipment, skin preparation and theatre discipline.
Know the purpose of common instruments and count them before and after surgery.
Pain control is pre-emptive and multimodal, with pain assessed and reassessed.
Drug availability and legal restrictions vary by species and country; check current national rules and guidance.

en.title: Farm animal medicine
en.short: Common cattle, sheep, goat, pig and poultry conditions: recognition, herd diagnosis and control.

sections.heading: Herd and animal
sections.text: Farm animal medicine treats the individual animal and the group. A herd is a group managed together. Herd-level medicine uses production records, housing, feeding and environment to explain why disease occurs. Recognition starts with changes in feed intake, milk yield, growth, mortality, coughing, diarrhoea or lameness. A production disease is caused mainly by management, feeding or housing, often with infection. For example, poor ventilation in a pig house irritates the airways and makes respiratory disease more likely. Wet bedding and foot problems follow the same pattern.

sections.heading: Common conditions
sections.text: Common cattle problems include mastitis (udder inflammation), lameness, bloat, ketosis, milk fever and displaced abomasum. Sheep and goats commonly show pregnancy toxaemia, hypocalcaemia, footrot and bloat. Pigs commonly show respiratory disease, diarrhoea, lameness and tail biting. Poultry commonly show coccidiosis, respiratory signs, egg peritonitis, leg weakness and heat stress. Many are multifactorial: several causes act together. Ketosis is a metabolic disease of early lactation when energy intake falls short of milk production. Diagnosis needs the history and group pattern, not just one sick animal.

sections.heading: Recognition and diagnosis
sections.text: Diagnosis at herd level combines records, inspection, clinical examination, necropsy and laboratory tests. A necropsy is a post-mortem examination. On a smallholder goat farm near Ibadan, Nigeria, Mama Ngozi reports lameness and poor growth. The veterinarian finds wet, crowded pens and lame goats with swollen feet. The group pattern and environment point to footrot and housing problems, not a single cause. Examining several animals and the pen is more useful than treating one goat.

sections.heading: Control and treatment
sections.text: Control works at animal and herd level. Isolate sick animals, correct housing, ventilation, bedding and feeding, and keep records. Vaccination, biosecurity and culling may be used where national guidance supports them. Treatment decisions follow current national veterinary guidance and the responsible use of antimicrobials. A withdrawal period is the time after treatment before milk, meat or eggs can be sold. It protects food safety. Ask a veterinarian and check the national regulator’s advice.

keyPoints: Farm animal medicine works at both individual and herd level.
Production, housing, nutrition and environment are major causes of disease.
Recognition uses records, clinical examination, necropsy and laboratory tests.
Common conditions include mastitis, lameness, metabolic disease, respiratory disease, diarrhoea and heat stress.
Treatment follows current national veterinary guidance and responsible antimicrobial use; this summary gives no doses.
Withdrawal periods protect food safety after treatment.

en.title: Companion animal medicine
en.short: Common dog and cat diseases: history, signs, diagnosis, management and prevention.

sections.heading: History and signs
sections.text: Companion animal medicine deals with dogs, cats and other companion animals. Take a full history: age, neuter status, diet, environment, vaccination and parasite control, previous illness, and the owner’s main concern. Ask about onset and change in appetite, water intake, urination, faeces, coughing, itching, lameness and behaviour. Examine the whole animal, not only the obvious problem. Clinical signs are abnormalities such as vomiting, pruritus (itching), pollakiuria (frequent small urinations) or weight loss. Many signs are nonspecific, so pattern and context matter.

sections.heading: Common conditions
sections.text: Common conditions include vomiting and diarrhoea, dermatitis (skin inflammation), dental disease, osteoarthritis (joint degeneration), obesity, epilepsy and heart disease. Cats often develop chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) and diabetes mellitus; dogs often develop hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) and pancreatitis (pancreas inflammation). Emergencies include collapse, breathing difficulty, severe pain, repeated vomiting and inability to urinate. A blocked cat cannot pass urine and needs urgent care. Do not give human medicines unless a veterinarian advises, because some are toxic to animals.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and management
sections.text: Diagnosis uses history, examination and selected tests. A minimum database often means complete blood count, biochemistry and urinalysis. Cytology, culture, imaging and infectious disease tests are added as needed. General management includes supportive care, fluids, nutrition, pain relief, parasite or infection control, and monitoring. Treatment protocols vary by country and change over time, so follow current veterinary guidance. Example: a 9-year-old cat with weight loss, increased thirst and urination is examined and tested; results suggest diabetes mellitus. The veterinarian explains monitoring, diet and insulin safety. No dose is given here.

sections.heading: Prevention and communication
sections.text: Preventive care includes vaccination, parasite control, dental care, weight management, neutering and screening for age-related disease. Schedules differ between countries and vaccines, so use national veterinary guidance. Owner communication should be clear and honest: explain findings, options, costs, prognosis and when to return. Check that the owner can give care at home and record consent. Educational only.

keyPoints: A full history and whole-body examination come before tests.
Common problems include vomiting, skin disease, dental disease, arthritis, obesity, kidney disease and diabetes.
A minimum database often means complete blood count, biochemistry and urinalysis.
Emergency signs include breathing difficulty, collapse, severe pain and inability to urinate.
Treatment protocols vary by country and must follow current veterinary guidance; no drug doses are given here.
Preventive care and clear owner communication improve adherence and welfare.

en.title: Infectious diseases of animals
en.short: Viral, bacterial and fungal animal diseases: spread, signs, diagnosis, control and reporting.

sections.heading: Infection and transmission
sections.text:
An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen such as a virus, bacterium, fungus or parasite. Many pathogens pass from one host to another. A reservoir is where the pathogen normally lives, such as cattle for brucellosis. A carrier shows no signs but can spread infection. The incubation period is the time from infection to first signs; it varies with pathogen, dose and host.

Transmission is direct by contact or droplets, or indirect by feed, water, equipment, people, vectors or the environment. Control targets each route.

sections.heading: Viral diseases
sections.text:
Foot-and-mouth disease affects cloven-hoofed livestock and causes vesicles, salivation and lameness; it is notifiable in many countries. African swine fever kills pigs and spreads by contact and contaminated meat; outbreaks have occurred in Africa, Europe, Asia and the Americas. Rabies spreads in saliva by bites and causes fatal nervous signs in mammals. Avian influenza affects birds and some strains infect people.

Diagnosis uses clinical signs and laboratory tests such as PCR, virus isolation or serology. Control uses vaccination where available, biosecurity, movement limits and culling.

sections.heading: Bacterial and fungal diseases
sections.text:
Anthrax spores survive in soil and cause sudden death, often with bleeding; it is zoonotic, so carcasses should not be opened. Brucellosis causes abortion and infertility in cattle, sheep and goats and can infect people through milk or birth fluids. Bovine tuberculosis is a chronic disease of cattle. Ringworm, or dermatophytosis, is a fungal skin infection of animals and people. Aspergillosis is a fungal respiratory disease, especially in stressed birds.

Diagnosis uses culture, microscopy, PCR or serology.

sections.heading: Control and reporting
sections.text:
A notifiable disease must be reported to the national veterinary authority when suspected. Lists differ by country, so check the current national list and WOAH information. Reporting allows tracing, movement controls, sampling and safe disposal.

Case: a poultry farmer in Nigeria sees sudden deaths and swollen heads. She reports at once, keeps visitors out and wears protective clothing. The veterinary service samples the flock and may confirm avian influenza. Control follows national guidance.

keyPoints: Infectious disease spread depends on the pathogen, host and route, and the incubation period varies.
Foot-and-mouth disease, African swine fever, rabies and avian influenza are important viral diseases; some are notifiable and some zoonotic.
Anthrax, brucellosis and bovine tuberculosis are important bacterial zoonoses; ringworm and aspergillosis are fungal examples.
Diagnosis combines history, clinical signs and laboratory tests such as PCR, culture and serology.
Control uses vaccination where available, biosecurity, isolation, movement control, vector control and safe disposal.
Suspected notifiable disease must be reported to the national veterinary service; lists differ by country.

en.title: Veterinary parasitology
en.short: Protozoa, helminths and arthropod parasites: life cycles, vectors, disease, diagnosis and control.

sections.heading: Parasite groups
sections.text: Parasitology studies organisms that live on or in a host and cause harm. Protozoa are single-celled parasites; examples are Babesia, spread by ticks and causing babesiosis, Trypanosoma, spread by tsetse flies and causing trypanosomiasis, and Eimeria, which causes coccidiosis. Helminths are worm parasites: nematodes such as Haemonchus, trematodes such as Fasciola, and cestodes such as Taenia and Echinococcus. Arthropods include ticks, mites, fleas, lice and flies; some are parasites and some are vectors carrying parasites between hosts.

sections.heading: Life cycles
sections.text: Direct life cycles need one host: eggs or larvae pass out and infect the same species after development. Indirect cycles need an intermediate host or vector, where it develops or multiplies. The definitive host carries the adult parasite; the intermediate host carries larval stages. Ticks transmit Babesia, tsetse flies transmit Trypanosoma, and snails are intermediate hosts for Fasciola. The cycle shows where control can act: pasture, water, vectors or housing. Warm, wet conditions favour many worm eggs and vectors, so local patterns differ by country and season.

sections.heading: Disease and diagnosis
sections.text: Disease depends on parasite load, age and immunity. Signs include poor growth, anaemia, diarrhoea, weight loss, jaundice and sudden death. Diagnosis uses history, clinical signs and laboratory tests: faecal flotation or sedimentation for eggs, blood smears for protozoa, and serology or PCR. Faecal egg counts estimate burden but do not identify every species. A Nigerian goat farm reports pale gums and poor growth in young goats. Faecal egg count and pasture history suggest Haemonchus contortus, the barber pole worm, which sucks blood. Confirm with laboratory support; treatment follows national guidance.

sections.heading: Control and resistance
sections.text: Control combines grazing management, clean water, quarantine, vector control and targeted treatment. Treat only animals that need it; use products correctly. Anthelmintic resistance is the inherited ability of worms to survive a dose that should kill them. It is detected by a faecal egg count reduction test. Integrated management, untreated animals and fewer treatments slow resistance. Patterns vary by climate, husbandry and country; check current guidance.

keyPoints: Protozoa, helminths and arthropods are the main parasite groups, and some arthropods are vectors.
Direct life cycles use one host; indirect cycles need an intermediate host or vector.
Diagnosis combines history, clinical signs and laboratory tests such as faecal egg counts and blood smears.
Control uses grazing management, hygiene, vector control and targeted treatment.
Anthelmintic resistance is inherited survival of worms at a dose that should kill them, tested by a faecal egg count reduction test.
Parasite patterns vary by climate and country, so check current national guidance.

en.title: Theriogenology: animal reproduction
en.short: Reproductive cycles, AI, pregnancy diagnosis, birth, disorders, herd fertility and neonatal care.

sections.heading: Anatomy and cycles
sections.text: Theriogenology is the study of animal reproduction. The female tract includes ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina and vulva. The male tract includes testes, epididymides, accessory glands and penis. Species differ: the cow has a firm, ringed cervix; the mare a soft cervix; the bitch a uterus with long horns and a short body. The estrous cycle is the recurring cycle of reproductive changes from one estrus to the next. It has follicular and luteal phases; estrus is the phase of mating receptivity. Cycle length and seasonality vary by species.

sections.heading: Mating and conception
sections.text: Mating is natural service. Artificial insemination (AI) places collected semen into the female tract. Success depends on detecting estrus, using fertile semen and correct technique. In cattle, standing heat is the main sign; in mares, teasing with a stallion is often used; in bitches, signs are less obvious. AI allows wider use of good sires but requires training and records. Semen collection, storage, transport and embryo transfer are regulated, and rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and birth
sections.text: Pregnancy diagnosis uses history, palpation, ultrasound and sometimes hormone or protein tests; timing and method differ by species. Normal birth, parturition, has three stages: cervical dilation, expulsion of the fetus and passing of the placenta. Dystocia is difficult birth. Causes are maternal, such as uterine inertia or a narrow pelvis, or fetal, such as malposition or oversize. Check progress, keep assistance clean, and call for help early. Newborns need warmth, clear airways, navel care and colostrum. Colostrum supplies antibodies; failure of passive transfer increases infection risk. Follow local guidance.

sections.heading: Disorders and herd fertility
sections.text: Common disorders include endometritis (uterine inflammation), pyometra (pus-filled uterus), retained fetal membranes, ovarian cysts, anestrus and abortion. In bitches, pyometra often follows estrus and is an emergency. Herd fertility is measured by submission rate (eligible cows served in a set period), conception rate, pregnancy rate, calving interval and services per conception. For example, if 100 eligible cows are served and 60 conceive, conception rate is 60 ÷ 100 = 60%. Low fertility prompts review of nutrition, heat detection, AI technique and disease. Reproductive procedures and notifiable disease rules vary by country; check national guidance.

keyPoints: Theriogenology covers reproductive anatomy, cycles, mating, pregnancy, birth and disorders.
The estrous cycle has follicular and luteal phases; estrus is mating receptivity.
AI success depends on estrus detection, fertile semen and correct technique.
Dystocia is difficult birth; causes may be maternal or fetal, and early help is important.
Common disorders include endometritis, pyometra, retained fetal membranes, ovarian cysts and anestrus.
Herd fertility uses submission rate, conception rate, pregnancy rate, calving interval and services per conception; conception rate = cows conceiving ÷ cows served × 100.

en.title: Herd health and preventive medicine
en.short: Planning herd health programmes: biosecurity, vaccination, parasites, nutrition, records and outbreak control.

sections.heading: Planning the programme
sections.text:
Herd health is the health of animals managed as a group. Preventive medicine aims to stop disease before it starts. Begin with goals and records: species, age, production, vaccinations, treatments, births and deaths. Records reveal patterns and guide decisions.

Biosecurity means measures that stop pathogens entering and spreading. Examples are quarantine of new animals, controlled visitors, cleaning and disinfection, and isolation of sick animals. Housing with good ventilation, dry bedding and sensible stocking density reduces stress. Balanced nutrition and clean water support immunity.

sections.heading: Vaccination and parasites
sections.text: A vaccination schedule is a plan of which groups to vaccinate and when. It follows risk, current national guidance and the product label. Keep vaccines cold, record batch numbers and check timing before expected risk. Parasite control is not only drugs. Combine grazing management, faecal egg counts and targeted treatment. This slows anthelmintic resistance, which is the ability of parasites to survive treatment. Review the plan with the veterinarian and adjust to farm conditions.

sections.heading: Outbreak investigation
sections.text: An outbreak is more cases than expected. Investigate. Confirm the problem, write a case definition (clear criteria for counting a case), count cases and keep a line list, a table of cases. Stop animal movement and isolate sick animals. Collect samples and send them to a laboratory. Trace contacts and sources. Notify the national veterinary authority if the disease is notifiable, meaning reporting is required by law. Control measures follow current national guidance. Review it later to improve the plan.

sections.heading: Economics of prevention
sections.text: Prevention costs money, so compare it with expected loss. Suppose 200 cattle need a yearly programme at 3 units each: 200 × 3 = 600 units.
