Without it, 10 in 100 may become ill: 0.10 × 200 = 20 cases. Each case costs 150 units: 20 × 150 = 3,000 units. If it prevents 80 in 100 of these losses, it avoids 0.80 × 3,000 = 2,400 units. Net benefit is 2,400 − 600 = 1,800 units. Use your own figures; prices vary.

keyPoints: Herd health plans start with goals, records and a clear case definition for problems.
Biosecurity prevents pathogens entering and spreading; housing and nutrition reduce stress.
Vaccination schedules follow risk, current national guidance and product labels.
Parasite control combines grazing management, faecal egg counts and targeted treatment to slow resistance.
Outbreak investigation confirms cases, stops spread, samples, traces contacts and notifies authorities when required.
Compare prevention cost with expected loss: net benefit = avoided loss − programme cost.

en.title: Veterinary public health, zoonoses and food safety
en.short: Covers zoonoses, meat and milk hygiene, inspection, foodborne disease, antimicrobial resistance and food safety law.

sections.heading: Zoonoses and One Health
sections.text:
Veterinary public health protects human health through animal health and food safety. A zoonosis is an infection or disease that passes between animals and people. Examples include rabies, brucellosis, bovine tuberculosis, salmonellosis, leptospirosis and cysticercosis. Some spread by contact, some by food, and some by vectors. The veterinarian recognises disease in animals, advises owners, vaccinates where available, and reports notifiable diseases (diseases the law requires you to report).

One Health is joint work by human, animal and environmental health professionals. One Health surveillance means sharing data on infections in people, animals and the environment. Guidance changes, so follow current national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Meat and milk hygiene
sections.text:
Meat and milk can carry pathogens from the live animal or from handling. Hygiene means keeping clean and cold, separating raw and cooked food, and preventing contamination from faeces, soil, equipment and people. Pasteurisation of milk kills many pathogens, and raw milk carries a higher risk. In the slaughterhouse, the veterinarian performs ante-mortem inspection of live animals and post-mortem inspection of the carcass and organs. The aim is to detect disease, residues and contamination, and to decide whether meat is fit for human consumption. National rules set what is condemned and how.

Case: a farmer in Kenya brings a cow that recently aborted and has swollen joints; the veterinarian suspects brucellosis, stops sale for slaughter, and advises testing and milk pasteurisation.

sections.heading: Foodborne disease and AMR
sections.text:
Foodborne disease is illness caused by contaminated food or water. Outbreaks are investigated by linking human cases to a food source and tracing it through the food chain. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria survive medicines that should kill them. In animals, AMR is encouraged by unnecessary antimicrobial use. Veterinarians should prescribe only when needed, follow withdrawal periods before meat or milk enters the food chain, and record use. Residues are traces of medicines or other chemicals left in food.

National food safety law sets standards for meat, milk and premises. Responsibilities differ by country, so check the current law and residue limits.

keyPoints: A zoonosis is an infection or disease transmitted between animals and people.
Ante-mortem inspection examines live animals; post-mortem inspection examines carcasses and organs.
Meat and milk hygiene depends on clean handling, cold storage and pasteurisation where appropriate.
Foodborne outbreaks are investigated by tracing human cases back through the food chain.
Antimicrobial resistance is reduced by prescribing only when needed, following withdrawal periods and recording use.
One Health surveillance shares data across human, animal and environmental health; food safety law differs by country, so check current national rules.

en.title: Veterinary ethics, law and professional practice
en.short: Professional codes, animal welfare law, consent, confidentiality, euthanasia and conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: Codes and law
sections.text: Professional codes are written rules of conduct. They require competence, honesty, animal welfare and public trust. Animal welfare law sets legal duties for cruelty, housing, transport, slaughter and research. The legal scope of veterinary practice differs by country. In Nigeria the Veterinary Council of Nigeria regulates practice; in the UK the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons does so. Their powers and the underlying statutes differ. Check your national veterinary council and current legislation before acting.

sections.heading: Consent and communication
sections.text: Animals cannot consent, so the owner or an authorised agent gives informed consent. This means explaining the diagnosis, options, likely benefits, risks, costs and alternatives in plain language, then recording the decision. Ask the owner to repeat back key points. In an emergency, provide necessary first aid and contact the owner as soon as possible. Consent for surgery, euthanasia or sharing records should be specific. Fees and estimates should be discussed early.

sections.heading: Confidentiality
sections.text: Client and animal records are confidential. Share them only with consent, for direct care, or when the law requires it. Legal exceptions vary by country and may include notifiable animal diseases (diseases the law says must be reported), animal bites, suspected cruelty and court orders. Tell owners at the start how records may be used. Keep records secure and accurate. Do not discuss cases in public. A breach can damage trust and may lead to professional discipline.

sections.heading: Euthanasia and conflicts
sections.text: Euthanasia is humane killing to end suffering. The decision weighs the animal’s welfare, prognosis and owner wishes, and the method used must be legal and humane. The veterinarian should give an honest opinion and avoid pressure. A conflict of interest is a personal or financial interest that may bias advice. Examples include selling medicines, owning a referral clinic or research funding. Disclose it and offer independent options. Case: a vet in Kenya owns the only local pharmacy; she should tell the owner about this interest and offer a written prescription so medicines can be sourced elsewhere.

keyPoints: Professional codes set standards of competence, honesty and animal welfare, but national law defines the legal scope of practice.
Check your national veterinary council and current legislation, because rules differ by country.
Animals cannot consent; obtain and record informed consent from the owner or authorised agent.
Keep client records confidential except where consent or law allows disclosure.
Euthanasia decisions should be based on animal welfare, prognosis, owner wishes and legal methods.
Disclose conflicts of interest and manage them so advice remains independent.

en.title: Advanced veterinary epidemiology and disease modelling
en.short: Measuring disease, study design, bias, outbreaks and models for animal and zoonotic disease.

sections.heading: Measuring disease frequency
sections.text: Prevalence is the proportion of animals affected at a point or period. Incidence is new cases in a population at risk over time. Cumulative incidence equals new cases divided by animals at risk at the start. Incidence rate uses animal-time at risk, such as cases per 100 pig-days. State the denominator, time window and case definition. Example: 50 new cases among 200 pigs over 10 days gives 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25, or 25%.

sections.heading: Study designs and bias
sections.text: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome together, so they show association, not cause. Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed animals and estimate risk. Case-control studies start with diseased and healthy animals and compare past exposure. Bias is systematic error away from the truth. Selection bias comes from how animals enter a study. Information bias comes from wrong measurement or recall. Confounding is a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome. Control it by design or analysis, such as randomisation.

sections.heading: Outbreaks and models
sections.text: An outbreak investigation sets a case definition, describes cases by time, place and animal, finds the source and recommends control. An epidemic curve plots cases over time. In the SIR model, animals are susceptible, infectious or recovered. R0 is the average secondary infections from one case in a fully susceptible population. The effective reproduction number is Rt = R0 × S, where S is the susceptible fraction. If R0 = 2 and S = 0.5, Rt = 1, so each case infects one other and cases stay level. Models inform policy but depend on assumptions.

sections.heading: Appraisal and policy
sections.text: Critical appraisal asks whether a study’s question, design, measurement and analysis support its conclusions. Check denominators, case definitions and confounding. For models, ask what is assumed about transmission, immunity and mixing, and whether uncertainty was tested. Examples include rabies in dogs, avian influenza in poultry and brucellosis in cattle. Models can compare vaccination, movement bans or culling, but do not replace field data. Follow current national veterinary guidance and the standards of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH, formerly OIE); WHO guidance matters for zoonoses.

keyPoints: Cumulative incidence = new cases ÷ animals at risk at the start.
Incidence rate uses animal-time at risk and needs a clear denominator and time window.
Cohort studies estimate risk; case-control studies suit rare diseases; cross-sectional studies show association.
Bias is systematic error; confounding is a third factor linked to exposure and outcome, controlled by design or analysis.
In the SIR model, Rt = R0 × S; if R0 = 2 and S = 0.5, Rt = 1.
Models support policy but depend on assumptions and field data, so follow current national veterinary guidance and WOAH (formerly OIE) standards; WHO guidance matters for zoonoses.

en.title: Veterinary research methods and dissertation design
en.short: Forming a veterinary research question, design, sampling, analysis, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Question and design
sections.text: A good veterinary research question is specific, answerable and useful. Use PICO for trials: population, intervention, comparison, outcome. For observational work use PECO, where exposure replaces intervention. Test the question against FINER: feasible, interesting, novel, ethical and relevant. Then choose a design. Cross-sectional studies measure prevalence at one time. Cohort studies follow groups and estimate incidence and risk. Case-control studies compare diseased and healthy animals and suit rare outcomes. Randomised trials test interventions but need random allocation and, where possible, blinding. A case series cannot prove cause.

sections.heading: Sampling and data
sections.text: Define the target population, sampling frame and unit of analysis: animal, farm or herd. Probability sampling supports generalisation; convenience sampling risks bias. Sample size depends on the question, expected effect, variability, power and significance level; calculate it with a statistician before collecting data. Plan data management early: use a data dictionary, unique identifiers, secure storage, backups and version control. Record missing values and pre-specify handling. For example, to compare lameness in cows on concrete versus deep litter, sample farms randomly within strata and cows within farms, and record floor type and locomotion score.

sections.heading: Analysis and qualitative
sections.text: Statistical planning starts with the primary outcome and a test that matches the design and data type. Check assumptions, such as normality, and plan sensitivity analyses. Avoid changing the main analysis after seeing results. Qualitative methods answer different questions, such as why farmers use antimicrobials or how owners view welfare. Purposive sampling selects information-rich cases. Interviews and focus groups need piloted guides, consent and secure transcripts. Thematic analysis groups repeated ideas into themes. Reflexivity means examining how the researcher affects findings. Mixed methods combine numbers and meanings.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Before data collection, obtain ethics approval. Human studies need consent and confidentiality. Animal studies need animal ethics committee approval and the 3Rs: replacement, reduction and refinement. Requirements vary by country and institution. Write the protocol with background, question, aims, design, sampling, sample size, analysis, ethics, timeline and budget. The dissertation adds results, discussion, limitations and references.

keyPoints: A strong question names the population, exposure or intervention, comparison and outcome, and passes the FINER test.
Choose the design that matches the question: cross-sectional for prevalence, cohort for incidence, case-control for rare outcomes, and randomised trials for interventions.

Sample size depends on effect size, variability, power and significance; to estimate a proportion with margin of error e, use n = Z² p(1−p)/e², where Z is the confidence-level value, before adjusting for finite population or design effects.
Plan data management before collection: data dictionary, unique identifiers, secure storage, backups and a missing-data plan.
Qualitative methods such as interviews and thematic analysis explain behaviour and beliefs, and typically use purposive sampling and reflexivity.
Obtain ethics and animal welfare approval before starting, and write the protocol and dissertation with clear aims, methods, analysis and limitations; requirements vary by country and institution.

en.title: Evidence-based veterinary medicine and evidence synthesis
en.short: Finding, appraising and combining veterinary evidence, and applying it to animals and herds.

sections.heading: Asking and finding
sections.text: Evidence-based veterinary medicine (EBVM) combines best available research evidence with clinical expertise, owner or farmer values and resources. Start with an answerable question using PICO: population, intervention, comparison and outcome. Search PubMed, CAB Abstracts and Google Scholar, but look first for guidelines and systematic reviews. Appraise each study for risk of bias: selection, performance, detection, attrition and reporting. In animals, record species, breed, age, production system and setting, because these affect whether evidence transfers.

sections.heading: Synthesis
sections.text: A systematic review follows a protocol, searches comprehensively, screens studies, assesses risk of bias and synthesises results. A meta-analysis is statistical pooling of comparable studies. Heterogeneity means differences between results beyond chance; a random-effects model is often used when present. Publication bias occurs when positive results are published more often; funnel-plot asymmetry suggests it. Example: two comparable studies report mean daily gain differences of +0.20 and +0.40 kg. With equal weights the simple pooled estimate is +0.30 kg per day ((0.20 + 0.40) ÷ 2). Real meta-analysis weights studies by precision.

sections.heading: Certainty and guidelines
sections.text: GRADE-style certainty rates how confident we are in an effect estimate: high, moderate, low or very low. It considers risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. Randomised trials start high and observational studies low, then are downgraded or upgraded. Guidelines combine evidence with judgement about benefits, harms, welfare, cost and local context. Check a guideline’s date, scope, species and conflicts of interest. A recommendation based on another species or country may be indirect evidence for your setting.

sections.heading: Applying evidence
sections.text: Apply evidence to animal and herd decisions with the owner, local data and welfare in mind. Absence of evidence is not evidence of no effect. Extrapolate cautiously between species, breeds and production systems. For example, lameness evidence from European confinement dairy farms may not fit a Nigerian pasture herd; check local prevalence, then pilot and monitor. Record outcomes and revise decisions as new evidence appears. National veterinary associations and international bodies publish guidance; confirm versions.

keyPoints: EBVM combines best evidence with expertise, owner values and resources.
Use PICO to build a searchable question and appraise risk of bias.
A systematic review follows a protocol; meta-analysis pools comparable studies.
With equal weights, a simple pooled estimate is (effect 1 + effect 2) ÷ 2; real meta-analysis weights by precision.
Heterogeneity and publication bias can make pooled estimates misleading.
GRADE-style certainty has four levels and five downgrading domains; absence of evidence is not evidence of no effect.

en.title: One Health and emerging zoonoses
en.short: Drivers, cross-sector surveillance, risk communication and outbreak response for zoonoses and AMR.

sections.heading: Drivers of emergence
sections.text:
One Health is the idea that human, animal and environmental health are linked and must be studied together. Most emerging infectious diseases are zoonoses: infections that pass from animals to people. Drivers include land use change and deforestation, which bring people and wildlife closer; livestock intensification; wildlife trade and markets; climate shifts that move vectors; travel and trade; and antimicrobial use.

Case: Nipah virus. Fruit bats carry it and feed on palm sap collected in open pots. People drink the raw sap, and pigs can amplify spread. Control follows the drivers: cover pots, test bats and pigs, and share data between health and veterinary services.

sections.heading: Surveillance across sectors
sections.text:
Surveillance is the continuous collection, analysis and sharing of health data. Cross-sector surveillance links human, livestock and wildlife data through joint outbreak investigation and laboratory networks. International reporting includes the WHO International Health Regulations (2005) and animal disease reporting by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Implementation and systems differ by country, so check current national guidance.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a One Health problem: resistant bacteria from animals, people and the environment mix. Integrated sampling and genomic comparison help trace spread.

sections.heading: Risk communication and response
sections.text:
Risk communication means giving clear, timely, honest information so people can act, and listening in return: address rumours, avoid blame. Outbreak response runs: detect and confirm; investigate using a case definition and active case finding; control; then evaluate.

Rift Valley fever in East Africa shows the chain. Heavy rain fills mosquito breeding sites, the virus spreads among livestock causing abortion storms, and people are infected by contact with animal tissues. Response combines animal vaccination, mosquito control, safe slaughter and public messaging. Follow current national or WHO guidance; this is not a drug protocol.

sections.heading: Case examples
sections.text: Rabies is controlled by mass dog vaccination plus post-exposure prophylaxis. Ebola virus is thought to have a bat reservoir; human outbreaks begin with contact with infected animals, then spread person to person. Colistin, a last-resort human antibiotic, has been widely used in livestock in some countries, showing how animal use affects human medicine.

keyPoints: One Health treats human, animal and environmental health as one linked system.
Most emerging infectious diseases are zoonoses.
Drivers include land use change, livestock intensification, wildlife trade, climate and antimicrobial use.
Surveillance must share data across human, livestock and wildlife sectors.
Risk communication is two-way and should avoid blame.
AMR spreads between animals, people and the environment, so it needs joint monitoring.
